headings.title: Introduction to Fluid Pressure
headings.content: Pressure is defined as the force exerted per unit surface area. When dealing with fluids—which include both liquids and gases—pressure behaves differently than it does in solid objects because fluid particles are free to move. A solid block resting on a table pushes downward only where it makes contact. In contrast, a fluid surrounds objects, transmitting forces equally in all directions at any given point. Understanding this basic concept is vital for midwives when administering intravenous infusions, managing respiratory therapy, or assessing physiological pressures within the human body.

headings.title: Pressure in Liquids
headings.content: Liquid pressure depends heavily on depth and density. As you go deeper into a liquid, the weight of the liquid layers pressing down from above increases, raising the overall pressure. This relationship is expressed through the formula $P = \rho g h$, where $\rho$ is density, $g$ is acceleration due to gravity, and $h$ is depth. Notably, liquid pressure acts equally in all directions at a specific depth and does not depend on the total volume or shape of the container. A narrow tube filled with water to a certain height exerts the exact same pressure at its base as a wide swimming pool at that same depth.

headings.title: Pressure in Gases
headings.content: Gases exert pressure through the continuous, rapid collision of gas molecules against the walls of their container. Unlike liquids, gases are highly compressible, meaning their volume changes easily when pressure or temperature changes. Atmospheric pressure is a prime example of gas pressure, caused by the weight of the air column stretching above the Earth's surface. At higher altitudes, the air becomes thinner, meaning there are fewer gas molecules above, which results in a lower atmospheric pressure.

headings.title: Mathematical Formulation and Measurement Units
headings.content: The standard international (SI) unit for pressure is the pascal (Pa), defined as one newton per square meter ($1 \text{ N/m}^2$). Because the pascal is a very small unit for many clinical and physical applications, kilopascals (kPa) are frequently used. In healthcare settings, blood pressure and gas pressures are often measured in millimeters of mercury (mmHg) using devices like sphygmomanometers. Understanding how to convert and interpret these units ensures accurate record-keeping and patient monitoring during clinical practice.

headings.title: Clinical Applications in Midwifery and Healthcare
headings.content: Fluid pressure principles govern numerous routine clinical procedures. Intravenous (IV) infusion relies on hydrostatic pressure; the fluid bag must be hung at a sufficient height above the patient's venous entry site so that gravity generates enough pressure to overcome venous blood pressure and drive fluid into the vein. Similarly, sphygmomanometers use gas and liquid pressure to occlude and measure arterial blood flow during antenatal assessments. Respiratory mechanics also depend on pressure gradients, as air flows into a mother's lungs during inspiration only when thoracic pressure drops below atmospheric pressure.
